cls: Antineoplastic - enzyme (pegylated L-asparaginase, derived from E. coli)
pharm: Pegylated form of E. coli L-asparaginase that depletes serum asparagine, selectively starving leukemic lymphoblasts (which cannot synthesize asparagine) of this amino acid; pegylation prolongs half-life and reduces immunogenicity versus native asparaginase.

Avoid; additive hepatotoxicity and pancreatitis risk
summary: Pegaspargase is a pegylated form of the enzyme L-asparaginase (derived from Escherichia coli) used as a component of multi-agent chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), including first-line treatment and treatment of patients who have developed hypersensitivity to native (non-pegylated) E. coli asparaginase. It works by hydrolyzing circulating asparagine to aspartic acid and ammonia; leukemic lymphoblasts cannot synthesize asparagine and depend on the extracellular supply, so asparagine depletion selectively impairs their protein synthesis and survival, while normal cells (which can make asparagine) are relatively spared. Pegylation extends the enzyme's half-life and reduces immunogenicity compared with native asparaginase, allowing less frequent dosing. The major serious toxicities are hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis, pancreatitis (which can be hemorrhagic or necrotizing), thrombosis and bleeding (from altered coagulation protein synthesis), hepatotoxicity, and glucose intolerance. Patients require monitoring of pancreatic enzymes, glucose, liver function, and coagulation, and must be observed for hypersensitivity reactions during and after each dose.
indications: First-line treatment of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) as a component of a multi-agent chemotherapy regimen
Treatment of acute lymphoblastic leukemia in patients who have developed hypersensitivity to native (non-pegylated) E. coli-derived L-asparaginase

moa: Pegaspargase is L-asparaginase (from E. coli) covalently conjugated to monomethoxypolyethylene glycol (PEG). The enzyme catalyzes the hydrolysis of the amino acid L-asparagine into aspartic acid and ammonia, depleting asparagine from the blood. Normal cells can synthesize asparagine from glutamate via asparagine synthetase, but leukemic lymphoblasts have little or no asparagine synthetase and depend on an exogenous supply of asparagine for survival. By depriving these cells of asparagine, pegaspargase inhibits their protein synthesis, DNA and RNA synthesis, and ultimately induces apoptosis, exerting a selective antileukemic effect. PEGylation prolongs the circulating half-life and decreases immunogenicity relative to native asparaginase, allowing less frequent dosing and use in some patients hypersensitive to the non-pegylated enzyme.

absolute: History of serious hypersensitivity reactions (including anaphylaxis) to pegaspargase
History of serious thrombosis with prior L-asparaginase therapy
History of pancreatitis with prior L-asparaginase therapy
History of serious hemorrhagic events with prior L-asparaginase therapy
monitor: Hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis during and after each dose
Serum amylase and lipase for pancreatitis
Coagulation parameters (fibrinogen, PT/aPTT, antithrombin) for thrombosis/bleeding

preg: Based on its mechanism and animal data, pegaspargase can cause fetal harm; avoid use during pregnancy. Verify pregnancy status before starting in females of reproductive potential and advise effective non-hormonal contraception during treatment and for at least 3 months after the last dose (asparaginase may reduce the efficacy of oral contraceptives via an interaction and altered hepatic synthesis, so a non-hormonal method is preferred).
lact: It is not known whether pegaspargase is excreted in human milk. Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in the breastfed infant, advise women not to breastfeed during treatment and for at least 3 months after the last dose.
renal: No specific renal dose adjustment is provided; pegaspargase is a large protein enzyme not eliminated by the kidneys, so renal impairment is not expected to significantly affect clearance. Monitor as clinically indicated.
hepatic: Use with caution in patients with hepatic impairment, as pegaspargase is itself hepatotoxic and can cause elevated transaminases, hyperbilirubinemia, hepatic steatosis, and impaired hepatic synthetic function (reflected in coagulopathy and hypoalbuminemia). Monitor liver function tests and coagulation parameters; interrupt or modify therapy for significant hepatotoxicity.

major: Oral (hormonal) contraceptives - asparaginase may reduce their effectiveness; use an additional or non-hormonal method during and after treatment
Anticoagulants/antiplatelet agents and NSAIDs - increased bleeding risk in the setting of asparaginase-induced coagulopathy
Other hepatotoxic chemotherapy agents - additive hepatotoxicity
moderate: Methotrexate - asparaginase can antagonize methotrexate's antifolate action (decreasing efficacy) or be used in sequence per protocol; observe protocol timing
Vincristine and corticosteroids (given concurrently in ALL regimens) - potential for increased toxicity (e.g., neuropathy, hyperglycemia); follow protocol sequencing
minor: Prednisone - protein-binding/hepatic effects may alter exposure
interactions.food: Not applicable (parenteral enzyme); maintain adequate nutrition and hydration.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol because of additive hepatotoxicity and increased risk of pancreatitis.
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor serum amylase/lipase, blood glucose, liver function tests, and coagulation studies (fibrinogen, antithrombin III, PT/aPTT); asparaginase lowers many serum proteins, which can affect interpretation of thyroid-binding and other transport proteins.

serious: Thrombosis (including cerebral sinus thrombosis) and serious hemorrhage
emergency: Severe upper abdominal pain radiating to the back with vomiting (pancreatitis)
Sudden severe headache, focal weakness, seizures, or visual changes (thrombosis/PRES)
Abnormal bleeding or signs of clot (limb swelling, chest pain, breathlessness)
Confusion or altered mental status (hyperammonemia/hepatic failure)

monitoring: Observe for hypersensitivity during and for at least 1 hour after each dose; have anaphylaxis treatment ready
Serum amylase and lipase at baseline and during therapy for pancreatitis; discontinue permanently if pancreatitis develops
Liver function tests and bilirubin; hold or modify for significant hepatotoxicity
Coagulation parameters including fibrinogen, antithrombin, PT/aPTT for thrombosis and bleeding
Blood glucose for hyperglycemia; manage with insulin as needed
Neurologic status for signs of cerebral thrombosis or PRES
counsel: This medicine is part of your leukemia treatment and is given by injection or infusion; you will be watched closely for at least an hour afterward
Tell your team immediately about itching, rash, swelling, dizziness, or trouble breathing during or after the dose (allergic reaction)
Report severe stomach pain spreading to your back, with nausea or vomiting, right away (possible pancreatitis)
Watch for and report leg swelling, chest pain, breathlessness, severe headache, weakness, or seizures (blood clots) and any unusual bleeding or bruising
Increased thirst, frequent urination, or confusion may signal high blood sugar - report these
Use a non-hormonal birth control method during and for 3 months after treatment, and do not breastfeed; avoid alcohol
pk: Asparagine depletion occurs rapidly after administration
Enzyme activity peaks shortly after dosing; depends on IV vs IM route
Mean elimination half-life approximately 5.5-7 days (much longer than native asparaginase)
Asparagine depletion sustained for roughly 14 days, supporting every-2-week dosing
Refrigerate at 2-8 C; do not freeze; do not shake; protect from light per label; discard if frozen
pearls: Pegylation gives a much longer half-life (~5.5-7 days) than native asparaginase, allowing dosing no more often than every 14 days and reducing immunogenicity

Hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis is a major risk - administer where resuscitation is available, observe >=1 hour after each dose, and switch to an Erwinia-derived asparaginase if a serious reaction occurs
Pancreatitis (including hemorrhagic/necrotizing) - monitor amylase/lipase and DISCONTINUE permanently if pancreatitis develops

Asparaginase impairs hepatic synthesis of clotting and anticoagulant proteins, causing BOTH thrombosis (including cerebral sinus thrombosis) and bleeding - monitor fibrinogen/antithrombin and coagulation
Hepatotoxicity and hyperglycemia are common - monitor LFTs and glucose and manage supportively
Use a NON-hormonal contraceptive (asparaginase can reduce oral contraceptive efficacy) during and for 3 months after therapy; avoid in pregnancy/lactation
missed: Pegaspargase is administered on a fixed schedule by a healthcare professional as part of a chemotherapy protocol. If a scheduled dose is missed, contact the treating oncology team; rescheduling is determined by the protocol - do not attempt to self-administer or alter the schedule.
overdose: Overdose is unlikely as doses are weight/body-surface-area based and given by professionals. In the event of overdose, there is no specific antidote; manage with supportive care and monitor closely for and treat hypersensitivity, pancreatitis, hepatotoxicity, coagulation disturbances (thrombosis/bleeding), and hyperglycemia.
